children: By Hannah Erin Lang and Sam Goldfarb
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh made it clear inflation is still a problem. Wall Street was left wondering how far the Fed will go to address it.

Stocks slumped and the 10-year Treasury yield settled above 5% for the first time since July 2007 after Warsh struck a decidedly hawkish tone in remarks following the central bank's decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.
"Inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said in remarks to reporters on Wednesday afternoon. He later added: "Today's action starts to show that we're serious about this."

At first, markets greeted the Fed's rate hike with relief; President Trump had argued rates were already too high, and investors had worried that Warsh would hesitate to tackle rising prices head-on. But soon after the new Fed chairman took to the podium Wednesday, stocks fell and the 10-year Treasury yield ticked up above 5% again.

"We have to be prepared that we are in a rate-hiking cycle," said Mike O'Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading. "You have uncertainty over the foreseeable future that warrants people being a little bit more defensive."

All three major U.S. stock indexes fell for the seventh time in the past eight sessions. The Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 1.2%, or 631 points. The S&P 500 fell around 0.4%, while the Nasdaq composite fell fractionally. The benchmarks were facing steeper declines before rebounding ahead of the close.
The Trump administration expressed its disappointment.

"Look, I think the president has been abundantly clear...on where he wanted interest rates to go," White House spokesman Kush Desai said during an interview on Fox News. "And certainly, today's rather unfortunate decision by the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates wasn't, from the administration's point of view, backed by a particularly compelling economic case."

In recent days, Wall Street came to see an interest-rate increase from the central bank as a near certainty. Investors were pricing in a 90% chance of a hike on Wednesday morning, and analysts warned of a sharp bond selloff if policymakers failed to deliver one.

Instead, the decision came in as expected-and a negative reaction took shape anyway. Markets responded as they often do when the Fed raises rates and signals inflation remains a concern: Yields rose and stocks fell.

At the start of 2026, many investors were banking on rate cuts. Then, the war in Iran scrambled inflation forecasts and jacked up fuel costs across the globe. Solid economic growth and the inexhaustible artificial-intelligence investing boom added to upward pressure on prices.

And over the past few months, an intensifying bond rout has placed even more pressure on Warsh and the Fed. Even an intervention from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proved insufficient in bringing down bond yields. Earlier this week, the yield on 10-year Treasurys touched a new 19-year high, climbing above 5% for the first time since it got there during a single session in 2023. Rising yields also put pressure on stock prices, in part by lifting borrowing costs across the economy.

Treasury yields, which rise when bond prices fall, largely reflect investors' expectations for short-term rates set by the Fed. Early Wednesday, they fell along with oil prices, which have been playing a critical role in shaping investors' inflation outlook. The 10-year yield initially didn't move much after the Fed's decision, but that changed as Warsh started speaking.
The yield was 5.020% in late afternoon trading, according to Tradeweb, up from 4.995% Tuesday. Brent crude, the international benchmark, still fell 2.7% to $105.83 a barrel.
Some analysts said that Warsh's commitment to fighting inflation still left bonds in a better position than if he had shown less resolve.

"I think the market is content with this, and it shows the Fed has a credible resolve to bring inflation down to 2%," said Will Compernolle, macro strategist at FHN Financial. Yields, he added, had stayed "within pretty narrow ranges all things considered."

But Wednesday's decision also turned traders' attention to the possibility of additional rate increases at the central bank's coming meetings in October and December. Interest rate futures showed a nearly 90% chance that the Fed will lift rates at least once more by the end of the year.
"Most people are bracing for further hikes," said Ben Emons, chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors. "It's never really a one-and-done."
